title: Parotid gland examination

guidelineVersions: Primary Care Notebook, Parotid gland palpation (last review 2018)

brief.scenario: You are a core surgical trainee in a head-and-neck assessment clinic. A 68-year-old patient has a swelling immediately in front of the right ear.
brief.task: Please examine the parotid region, assess for important complications and explain your findings and immediate plan to the examiner. No instruments or imaging are required. The examiner will provide physical findings when you describe a manoeuvre. You may ask brief relevant questions. You have 9 minutes.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: a systematic parotid examination must recognise a gland lesion, assess regional nodal disease, facial nerve function and suspicious skin lesions.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: a smooth painless pre-auricular mass can still be malignant; never conclude it is benign without checking the facial nerve, nodes and skin.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: introduce, verify identity, consent, expose head/neck appropriately, then inspect from front and behind.

flow: 0:00–1:00 Introduce, consent, hand hygiene, comfort and expose head and neck.
1:00–3:00 Inspect both parotid regions, external ear, overlying skin and symmetry; palpate the lump gently and describe size, borders, tenderness, consistency, mobility and skin fixation.

3:00–4:30 With permission, inspect the oral cavity, the parotid duct opening and the tonsil/soft palate for medial displacement by a deep-lobe mass; assess salivary flow if appropriate; compare the opposite parotid and both submandibular glands.
4:30–6:30 Test all facial nerve functional groups and assess cervical lymph nodes; inspect scalp, temple and external ear for skin primaries.
6:30–9:00 Present coherent findings, identify red flags, communicate concern proportionately, propose urgent head-and-neck assessment, ultrasound and image-guided cytology as directed by specialists.

grid.label: Safety, introduction and consent
grid.fail: Starts examining without consent or hygiene
grid.pass: Introduces self/role, confirms identity, obtains permission, hand hygiene and appropriate exposure
grid.high: Checks discomfort, offers chaperone where appropriate, preserves dignity and adapts examination

grid.label: Inspection of parotid region and skin
grid.borderline: Looks at one side but misses skin or asymmetry
grid.pass: Inspects front and behind, both glands, skin, ear and previous scars
grid.high: Recognises temple scar as potential cutaneous primary and deliberately examines scalp/ear

grid.label: Lump characterisation
grid.pass: Examines size, site, surface, consistency, tenderness, mobility and fixation
grid.high: Separates gland from node and explains which findings increase concern

grid.label: Duct and intraoral examination
grid.fail: Omits mouth, Stensen duct and oropharynx
grid.pass: Describes cheek retraction and inspection of the duct opening opposite the upper second molar, the oral cavity, and the tonsil/soft palate for medial displacement by a deep-lobe mass
grid.high: Links purulent discharge or meal-related pain to infection/obstruction but avoids overdiagnosis

grid.label: Facial nerve examination
grid.pass: Tests forehead, tight eye closure, smile/show teeth and puffed cheeks bilaterally
grid.high: Identifies asymmetry as urgent red flag, documents baseline and protects eye if closure weak

grid.label: Cervical nodes and skin primary
grid.pass: Palpates cervical/preauricular nodes and examines ear, temple and scalp for previous/current lesions
grid.high: Explains possible spread of head/neck cutaneous SCC to intraparotid nodes without assuming diagnosis

grid.label: Presentation and differential
grid.pass: Summarises objective findings, acknowledges uncertainty and gives benign/malignant and salivary/lymph node differentials
grid.high: Prioritises malignancy risks while explaining inflammatory and obstructive alternatives

grid.label: Referral and investigations
grid.fail: Suggests reassurance alone despite red flags
grid.borderline: Suggests non-urgent scans despite concerning findings
grid.pass: Recommends urgent ENT/head-and-neck referral, ultrasound and specialist-led needle sampling
grid.high: Escalates promptly for facial weakness or rapid progression and discusses MDT pathway

grid.label: Communication and safety-netting
grid.pass: Explains why assessment is required, avoids diagnosing cancer and advises return for weakness, fast growth or infection
grid.high: Checks understanding and gives clear safety-netting and follow-up ownership

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Hello. I am the doctor. I need to feel the lump now.

fail.speaker: patient
fail.text: All right, but it is a bit sore when pressed.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It looks like a swelling in front of your right ear.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: There is a visible swelling over the right parotid tail and a healed scar over the right temple.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What would you examine?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I would press it to see whether it is tender.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: It is a 2.5 cm firm, minimally tender mass. What else?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: If it moves, that is reassuring. I think it is probably a benign parotid lump.

fail.speaker: patient
fail.text: My daughter is worried about it.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: These are usually harmless. I do not think we need to worry.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Would you assess cranial nerves?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I would ask the patient to smile.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: There is reduced movement at the right corner of the mouth. What is your interpretation?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It may be age-related; I would not change the plan.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Would you inspect elsewhere?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I would probably feel the neck briefly.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: A small firm right upper cervical node is present.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Would you examine inside the mouth?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: No, that is not necessary for a lump on the outside.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: The temple scar is old, so I would not connect it with this lump.

fail.speaker: patient
fail.text: Should I contact anyone if my face gets weaker?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I do not think that will happen; there is no need to contact anyone.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Please summarise.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Probably a benign salivary swelling. Routine review.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Curveball: the patient says it has doubled in size over the last two weeks. What now?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: That does not change much. I would organise a routine ultrasound in a few months.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello, I am the core surgical trainee. Could I confirm your name? I have been asked to examine the swelling by your right ear. I will look at the face and neck, feel gently, examine the inside of your cheek, and check facial movements. Is that okay?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Yes. Please be gentle.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Of course. Tell me if anything hurts. I will clean my hands and compare both sides.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: From the front and behind I would inspect the parotid outlines, ears, overlying skin, scars and asymmetry.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: There is a visible swelling over the right parotid tail. The skin is intact. A healed scar lies over the right temple.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would record the scar and ask what operation was done there after finishing examination.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: May I gently feel the lump? I would assess its size, site, borders, consistency, tenderness, mobility relative to skin and deeper tissues, and warmth.

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Yes.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: It is 2.5 cm, firm, poorly mobile and minimally tender; no skin warmth.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would document those findings without assuming a benign lesion.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: May I look inside your mouth? I would inspect the cheek opposite the upper second molar for the parotid duct opening, check for discharge or intraoral abnormality, and look at the tonsil and soft palate on that side to see whether a deeper part of the gland is pushing them inwards.

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Yes, go ahead.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: The mucosa is normal, there is no pus at the duct opening, and the tonsil and soft palate are not displaced.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: That does not suggest acute suppurative parotitis, though it does not settle the cause of the mass.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Please raise your eyebrows, shut your eyes tightly, smile and show your teeth, then puff out your cheeks.

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Like this?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: There is mild weakness of the right lower facial movements; forehead elevation and eye closure are preserved.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: There is right-sided lower facial weakness; in the setting of a parotid mass I would treat this as concerning and arrange urgent specialist review.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I would palpate the cervical and preauricular nodes and examine the scalp, ear and temple for skin lesions or scars.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: There is a small firm ipsilateral level II node and a healed temple excision scar.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Could I ask what was excised from your temple?

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: They said it was a squamous skin cancer last year.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: This is a firm poorly mobile parotid-region mass with facial weakness and a cervical node. A salivary tumour or metastatic node is possible; I cannot distinguish the cause by examination alone.

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Does that old skin cancer mean this is cancer too?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Not necessarily. But some skin squamous cancers can spread to nodes around the parotid, so it is important that the team knows your pathology history.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Curveball: the patient says it doubled in size over two weeks.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: That rapid growth increases concern. I would discuss it urgently with the head-and-neck or ENT team today, rather than book a routine review.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The specialist team can arrange ultrasound and appropriate image-guided needle sampling, with imaging and MDT planning as needed.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: If facial weakness worsens, the eye will not close, or swelling rapidly progresses, seek urgent assessment. I will ensure the referral is made and its outcome followed up.

pass.speaker: patient
pass.text: Thank you; I would like to know what happens next.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I will explain the referral and make sure you know whom to contact.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Good morning. I am the core surgical trainee. May I confirm your name? I want to examine both sides of your face and neck, inside the cheek, and the facial muscles because those structures help locate the swelling safely. Please stop me if anything is uncomfortable.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: That is fine, but the lump worries me.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I can see why. I will explain what I find, and I will be clear about what examination can and cannot tell us.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I am comparing the parotid contours and inspecting the ear, temple, scalp margin, overlying skin and scars, both face-on and from behind.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Right parotid-tail asymmetry and a healed right temple scar; skin not inflamed.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I note the scar because a prior head-and-neck skin lesion may be relevant to an apparent parotid mass.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I will palpate from the normal side first, then describe the exact site, 3-dimensional size, surface, consistency, tenderness, mobility, and whether the skin is tethered. I will ask you to clench your teeth so I can feel the gland against the masseter, and I will compare the opposite parotid and both submandibular glands.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: It is slightly uncomfortable.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Right mass 2.5 cm, firm, poorly mobile, minimally tender, no heat, no skin tethering.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: This is not typical of simple acute inflammation; poor mobility is concerning but cannot alone establish malignancy.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: With permission I will inspect the oral mucosa and Stensen duct opening opposite the upper second molar, looking for obstruction, inflammation or pus, and check whether the tonsil or soft palate is pushed medially by a deep-lobe mass.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: Yes.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Normal mucosa, no duct pus or visible calculus; tonsil and soft palate not displaced.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would still ask separately about meal-related pain or swelling, because an unobstructed-looking duct does not exclude intermittent obstruction.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Please lift both eyebrows, close both eyes tightly while I gently test resistance, smile, show your teeth and puff your cheeks. I am comparing each movement side-to-side.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Forehead and eye closure preserved, but subtle right lower facial weakness.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: There is asymmetrical lower facial function. I would document a baseline and specifically report it in the urgent referral; if eye closure became deficient I would institute eye protection and escalate. Forehead sparing here does not make this an upper motor neurone or stroke pattern; a parotid lesion can involve only the lower branches of the facial nerve.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I will palpate the preauricular, parotid-tail and cervical nodal regions, and inspect the scalp, temple and pinna for a cutaneous primary.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Small firm right upper cervical node and old right temple scar.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Was the temple lesion removed, and were you told what it was?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: Squamous cell cancer, about a year ago.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Thank you. I would request the histology record and include that detail explicitly in the handover.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: My findings are a firm poorly mobile right parotid-tail mass, subtle ipsilateral lower facial weakness and a firm cervical node, with previous cutaneous SCC of the same-side temple. The differential includes primary salivary neoplasm and nodal metastatic cutaneous SCC; benign salivary disease is also possible.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: Are you telling me the old cancer has come back?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: No. This examination raises concern, but only specialist investigation can establish what it is. We will not label it as recurrence without evidence.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Curveball: the swelling has doubled in the last two weeks.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would contact the head-and-neck team urgently today and document the change, facial findings and previous SCC. This should not be left to routine outpatient follow-up.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I would expect specialist ultrasound and image-guided needle cytology/biopsy as appropriate, review of prior histology, and further imaging or MDT review guided by findings.

high.speaker: patient
high.text: What if my mouth gets more crooked while I wait?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Please seek urgent medical assessment for worsening facial weakness, difficulty closing the eye, severe pain or rapidly increasing swelling. We will give you clear contact details and follow up the referral.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Could you tell me what you understand about the next step, so I can correct anything unclear?

high.speaker: patient
high.text: You are concerned enough to arrange a prompt specialist check, but it is not yet a diagnosis.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Exactly. I will make sure the team receives the full findings and your previous pathology information.

failures.move: Fails to examine or act on new facial nerve weakness in a parotid mass
failures.consequence: delayed recognition of potentially invasive disease.

failures.move: Routes rapidly enlarging mass plus weakness to routine review without urgent specialist escalation
Dismisses ipsilateral previous cutaneous SCC and firm cervical node without considering metastatic disease
Gives firm reassurance that the mass is benign despite red flags
failures.consequence: misleading information that may deter reassessment.

recovery.when: If you have described the lump but not yet checked the facial nerve and cervical nodes
recovery.line: I have described the lump, but I must now check the facial nerve and cervical nodes before making a safe assessment.

recovery.when: If the new detail about rapid growth emerges
recovery.line: That new detail about rapid growth changes the urgency; I would contact the specialist team today rather than continue the routine plan.

knowledge.fact: Pain, rapid growth, fixity to surrounding structures, nerve involvement or neck metastasis all suggest malignancy in a salivary lump, and such patients should be seen in a rapid-access neck lump clinic.
The deep lobe may be seen and felt through the mouth and may displace the tonsil if enlarged; regional lymph nodes should be palpated for secondary deposits.
Ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration cytology is recommended for all salivary tumours.
Squamous cell carcinoma in the parotid is commonly a metastasis from skin cancer and first presents as a discrete parotid lump.
NICE NG12 uses unexplained/persistent neck lumps in its site-specific suspected-cancer referral recommendations; this is not a dedicated parotid examination standard.
NICE advises explaining uncertainty, alternative diagnoses and the reason for suspected-cancer referral.
Consent, dignity and clear communication are professional duties.

recall.think: gland tumour versus intraparotid node; screen for cutaneous SCC, facial nerve deficit and neck nodes.
recall.say: “I cannot diagnose the cause by examination alone.”
do: examine both glands → lump → duct → facial nerve → neck nodes → scalp/temple/ear.

numbers.meaning: station 9 + 1 minutes; no numeric malignancy risk cut-off is required.

recall.trap: calling a smooth, painless mass benign before testing facial nerve.
recall.finish: urgent head-and-neck referral for red flags, ultrasound/sampling via specialist pathway, safety-net and documented follow-up.

partner.opening: Please examine the parotid region, assess for important complications and explain your findings and immediate plan to the examiner.
partner.actorBrief: “I have this swelling in front of my right ear, and it is bothering me.” Cooperative but worried. Do not volunteer the old skin cancer or recent rapid growth unless asked / cued. Keep the answers identical across performance bands. If asked about old scar: “Squamous cell skin cancer was removed from my right temple a year ago.”

reveals.finding: right parotid-tail swelling; healed temple scar; no skin inflammation.
2.5 cm firm poorly mobile minimally tender lump; no warmth; no tethered skin.
normal mucosa, no visible pus at Stensen duct, tonsil and soft palate not displaced.
mild right lower facial weakness; forehead elevation and eye closure preserved.
firm small right upper cervical node.

Provide physical findings only after a corresponding manoeuvre is stated. Reveal the growth curveball at the scheduled time even if candidate never asks. Distinguish a communication omission from a critical safety failure.

curveballs.prompt: At approximately 7:15, after presentation: “I forgot to say it has doubled in size in the last two weeks.”
curveballs.safeAnswer: That rapid growth increases concern. I would discuss it urgently with the head-and-neck or ENT team today, rather than book a routine review.

curveballs.prompt: After discussing investigations: “Are you telling me the skin cancer has returned?”
curveballs.safeAnswer: Expect honest uncertainty, not false reassurance.
